Several patterns on one body – bricks round the sides, knurling on the top – are layers: “Layer” beside the first adds one, and picking is switched on for it at once; click the faces it should get. Every further layer goes only on its own faces, the first on all the others. The tabs show one layer at a time with its settings, “Remove this layer” takes one away. All layers are made together on the body under the texture, so changing one or taking the texture off works as for a single pattern. A text needs no faces as a layer: it goes where it is put. Under “Mais” you choose where the pattern goes: outer and inner walls, how far the bottom and the top stay smooth (a smooth bottom keeps the body flat on the bed), a band of the height, and whether sharp edges stay smooth. Next to everything that stays smooth, the pattern fades in gently; “Distância de transição” sets over how many millimetres. The smaller it is, the closer the pattern comes to an edge; a pattern standing out runs out right up to it. On the flat sides of an angular body like a cube it ends at a straight border that far away instead: grooves and diamonds stop with a short wall, and only whole bumps stay. “Perfil” shapes the cross-section of a groove or joint: pointed and flat come out exactly, round in as many steps as “Nível de detalhe” gives it. Besides “Ranhuras”, “Serrilhado”, “Colmeia” and “Saliências” there are more patterns. “Células” are irregular cells like paving stones or dried clay; their joints are cut cleanly as the honeycomb's are, and another “Disposição” lays them out anew. “Tricô”, “Corda” and “Trançado de vime” copy knitted stitches, a wound rope and a basket of stakes and weavers; they start raised and round, at the size of their models. “Granulado” roughens the surface finely, as if blasted; the grain lies in space, without a seam or stretching. “Imagem” takes a grey picture as a height map: one of the ready ones such as wood, topography or terrazzo, or your own with “Carregar sua própria imagem…”. Light becomes the full depth; “Largura do ladrilho” sets how wide a tile is, and under “Ladrilhos” the tiles repeat, mirror or are staggered. A dark drawing on a transparent ground, such as black lines in an SVG, counts by its lines: they become the full depth. With “Uma vez” the image is pressed on a single time, like a label: “Na volta (°)” and “Altura (%)” place its middle as for a text, “Largura da imagem” sets its width, and the surface beside it stays smooth. With faces picked, it always lands on them, even where “Na volta (°)” and “Altura (%)” aim past them. “Carbono (sarja)” lays carbon fibre woven in twill onto the body: upright bands and crossing bands, over and under each other, one band on from band to band, so the familiar diagonal shows. “Trama” chooses “Sarja 2/2”, the even weave of most carbon parts, or “Sarja 2/1” and “Sarja 3/1”, where the upright bands show long and the crossing ones short. “Largura da faixa” sets how wide the upright bands are; “Largura da faixa transversal” makes the crossing ones wider or narrower for an uneven weave (0: as wide). Round a body the band width is rounded a little so the weave closes without a seam. The single fibres are far too fine for a print: the bands with their crossings are what shows. “Tijolos” lay a brick wall onto the body, with joints sunk in like mortar. “Amarração” chooses how the bricks are laid: “Junta amarrada” as most walls are, “Junta a prumo”, or with short bricks between the long ones (“Amarração inglesa”, “Amarração inglesa cruzada”, “Amarração flamenga”). “Comprimento do tijolo” and “Altura da fiada” count from joint to joint and are rounded a little so that whole bricks fit: round a cup, from edge to edge of a box's side and from the bottom to the top; “Largura da junta” says how wide the joints are. Under “Mais”, “Tijolos irregulares (%)” lets every brick lie a little deeper, as in an old wall. “Squares” and “Triangles” lay tiles of one size in a grid onto the body, raised or pressed in, their walls cut steep and clean; the triangles stand in rows, pointing up and down in turn. “Square size” or “Triangle size” and “Gap” stay exactly as you set them – squares of 3.2 mm, 3.2 mm apart, are eight lines of a 0.4 mm nozzle each and print cleanly. The grid is centred on every face; round a round body the gap is rounded a little so that a whole number goes round. With “From the bottom edge” the first row starts right at the bottom edge and reaches down into the first layer, where a brim holds it. For tiles on only the lower half of two sides, pick the two faces and put a helper body over the upper half with “Mantém a área sem textura” under “Máscara de textura” (see below). Under “Mais”, the “Perfil” “Pontiagudo” makes pyramids of them, “Arredondado” and “Semicircular” cushions. “Half-timbering” and “Stone wall” are made for model buildings, such as the houses of a model railway or a diorama. “Half-timbering” raises beams out of the wall, the plaster between them lying lower: posts “Panel width” apart, a sill and a plate to every storey of “Storey height”, and “Rails per storey” across it. “Bracing” chooses how much wood the panels hold: “Braces” lean towards the middle from both ends, “St Andrew's crosses” sit under the lowest rail, “Corner braces” in the top corners, and “Mixed” puts braces at the ends with crosses and corner braces between, as on many old houses. “Beam width” and “Beam height” make the beams wide and deep, “Wood grain (%)” gives them a grain: 0 % none, below 50 % more and finer lines, above it two wide, deep grooves – from planed wood to rough planks. As with bricks, panels and storeys are rounded a little so that whole ones fit, from the bottom edge up. “Stone wall” lays an old wall of stones of different sizes in rough courses, the mortar joints lower and every stone bulging a little by its own amount. “Roundness (%)” goes from broken stone with sharp edges (0 %) to rounded field stones (100 %); “Size variation (%)”, “Largura da junta” and “Disposição” say how different the stones are, how wide the joints and how they lie. Both are shape only, in one colour, so “Pattern as its own part” can make the beams or the stones a part of their own in a second colour. The pattern “Rachaduras (kintsugi)” grows cracks across the surface as in kintsugi, with kinks, branches and a width that tapers towards the end. “Ponto de partida” tells where they begin: at the top rim of a vase or a cup, at the bottom, from the rim to the middle of a plate, or anywhere; under “Tipo” they become lightning. With “Preenchimento de ouro como peça separada” the notch is filled by a part of its own in gold, for a second filament; it goes along when you change or remove the texture. Under “Mais” you set branches, zigzag and chipped edges, and another “Variação” throws the cracks anew. “Casca de árvore” lays a tree's bark round a log: “Carvalho”, “Pinheiro”, “Abeto”, “Bétula” or “Faia”, each at its own size and depth. “Veio da madeira” makes the body a piece of wood: under “Madeira” choose oak, ash, beech, pine or walnut, under “Corte” a log without its bark or a board, flat-sawn with its arches or quarter-sawn with straight lines. “Largura dos anéis” makes the grain fine or coarse. With “Anéis de crescimento nas extremidades” the ends of a log show the annual rings, and they match the grain on its sides: the rings run through the whole body as in a real piece of wood. Under “Mais” you add “Nós”, and the rings bend round them. With the pattern “Texto (colado)” you stick a text onto the body like a label pressed on: the surface is unrolled round the place, so the letters keep their size on a vase's belly, on a slanted wall or over the edge of a box. "Around" (0° is the front, 90° the right) and "Height" in % along the axis say where it goes; with the axis on X or Y, 0° is the top - that puts the text on a flat plate. “Direção” engraves it or raises it. Over a real corner it tears like a sticker; the status message says so then. “Letras de cima para baixo” stacks the letters top to bottom here too. With faces picked, the text always lands on them, even where “Na volta (°)” and “Altura (%)” aim past them. To keep part of the body smooth, or to texture only a part, use a helper body: put a box, a cylinder or a sphere where it should be, select it and choose under “Máscara de textura” either “Mantém a área sem textura” or “Textura só aqui”. It turns transparent, and it counts when the other body gets its texture, also while it is hidden. Hide or delete it before printing. The result is a mesh like an imported model, and it keeps the body it was made on. Select it later, also after saving, and the card shows the settings it was made with: change them and click “Alterar textura”, and the texture is made again on that body, where and as large as the textured body stands now. “Remover textura” gives the plain body back. Mask bodies count again when the texture is changed: hide them rather than delete them if you may change it later. Undo takes back each of these steps as well. For a print in two colours, switch on “Pattern as its own part”, with any pattern: the pattern becomes a part of its own, and “Colour of the pattern” gives it its colour – to begin with one that stands out against the body, the next time the one you chose last. Out of the body, the part is what stands out, and the body stays as it was; into the body, the body gets the pattern cut in and the part fills the cut up to the surface, like the gold of the cracks. Both go together in a bundle: they move together, each keeps its colour, and a 3MF has them as two parts for the slicer. Change or remove the texture as before; the pattern part goes along. With several layers, all have to go the same way, out of the body or into it; a pattern going both ways stays one with the body.

For a print in several colours, “Paint” colours parts of a body right in the design: a face, a round wall, the inside of a hole, a round patch or an area you draw round. It works like the paint tools of the slicers, but the paint is saved with the design. Select one body and click “Paint” in the “Modificar” group, next to “Textura de superfície”. The panel offers the colours of your design, and “A colour of your own” mixes one of your own. Then paint in the view with one of three tools: “Fill”: a click fills the face up to its sharp edges, like the bucket of a paint program: the top of a box, the wall of a cylinder, the floor of a pocket or the inside of a hole, each in one click. “Stop at edges sharper than” says how sharp an edge has to be to stop the fill; at 90° it runs over the edges of a box. “Circle”: a click lays a round patch of the “Diameter” set onto the surface, centred where you click, on a curved surface too. It stops at the body's sharp edges and never comes through on the back of a wall. “Lasso”: hold the mouse button and draw round an area. What you see inside the shape is painted; the back of the body behind it is not. A box painted with the three tools: its top filled in yellow, a white circle on the front and a green star drawn round on the side, the Paint panel beside it. “Eraser” takes the paint off again with the same tools, “Clear all” takes all of it off at once. Every stroke is a step of its own, so Ctrl+Z takes the last one back. Between strokes the right mouse button turns the view as always; “Done” or Esc closes the panel. The edges of a circle or a lasso are cut into the body's mesh, so a circle on the face of a box is round, not a few triangles, and the body stays closed. The paint belongs to the body: it moves and turns with it, stretches with it when you resize it, and a stroke that finds nothing any more after a change is left out. A 3MF export writes the paint as painted faces, which OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio and PrusaSlicer print with their filaments (see Files and saving); an OBJ keeps the colours too, an STL stays one colour. A group cut into one body, a box with its holes for instance, is painted as one body: paint it after cutting the holes, and its paint stays when you change the group in an open group. The parts of a bundle are painted one by one. A painted body that you group with others keeps its paint as a part and shows it again when you ungroup it. An imported mesh that is not closed is painted on its own triangles.

The “Vaso” is a body of its own for vases, pots and lampshades. Its measures are under “Propriedades”, its form and pattern on the card “Forma e padrão”; all of it can be changed at any time, also after saving: “Formato”: bottle, bellied, bowl with neck, barrel, cylinder or funnel. The height and the widest diameter are the shape's own measures: drag the handles, or type “Diâmetro” and “Altura”. “Seção transversal”: a circle, a polygon with rounded corners or a wave (soft, pointed, arches or fins). “Torção (°)” turns it up the height, “Oscilação (°)” lets it swing back and forth. “Construção”: “Maciça (modo vaso)” is for the slicer's vase mode (also called spiralize): the slicer prints one wall in a spiral and leaves out the top and the infill, so the body is drawn solid. “Oca, com parede” gives a real wall and bottom for a normal print. With “Fundo” at 0 mm the hollow vase has no bottom: a tube open at both ends, for bells, mouthpieces and pipes. “Padrão”: a new vase is plain. To choose from are grooves, stripes, Voronoi cells or facets (low poly) on the outside, in a band of the height if you like; they belong to the vase and stay editable with it. “Seção transversal no topo” blends the cross-section into a second one up the height, say from a circle at the bottom to a hexagon at the top. “Desenhar o vaso”, high up in the vase's settings, opens a large window of its own over the work area: in it you draw the vase yourself, in real millimetres. You move it by its title bar and make it larger from its corner; the vase in the view follows every change. “Formato” shows it from the side: drag the points, the top one sets the height, the widest one the diameter; “Alça” gives a point an angle, “Canto” a kink. “Seção transversal” shows the cross-section from above, and the “Simetria” mirrors or repeats what you draw. “Torção” draws the twist as a curve up the height. An SVG file from a drawing program becomes the cross-section or the body form, the mesh of a model vase (STL, 3MF, OBJ) the body form. A photo of a vase can go behind the drawing to trace, or “Usar contorno” takes its outline. “Traçar” does the same with settings: “Limiar” for how clearly the object must stand out from the background, “Pontos” (3 to 40) and “Canto a partir de”; the new body form shows in red over the photo first and becomes the vase's with “Aplicar”. Where the vase stands before a busy background (a shelf, a room), the search does not find it; then the “Laço magnético” catches it: click roughly round the vase, between two clicks the line follows the edge by itself, and a click on the first point, a double click or Enter closes it. The body form then comes from the lasso; “Descartar laço” lets the search look again. One drag of the mouse is one step of undo; while you drag, the view shows the vase roughly. The card “Fundo e parede” holds what the body needs besides its form. On a hollow vase: drain holes with a slope towards them, a hollow foot, an open wall (“Parede perfurada”: Voronoi, honeycomb, diamonds or circles, for lanterns and baskets) and a “Cúpula de luminária”, hanging, standing on a socket or over an LED puck. On a solid vase, “Modo vaso reforçado” cuts fine slits through which the slicer prints ribs inside or a double wall in its vase mode, in one go. Recesses for rubber feet go with either. “Precisa reter água” raises the wall and bottom of a hollow vase to at least 1.6 mm. On the card “Acessórios” the vase gets its accessories. “Pés” can be moulded on, so they are part of the vase, or made to plug in, with sockets in the bottom; a stand holds the vase from below. A “Prato” catches the water, or hides in the foot. A hollow vase can take an “Inserto”: a plant insert, one with a water store for a pot that waters itself, a holder for stems or water tubes. A “Tampa” slips over the rim, snaps into a groove or screws onto a thread in the wall. As a “Tampa de bule” the top of the vase itself becomes the lid, as on a teapot: “Altura da tampa” (or “Vaso até · tampa a partir de”, from the bottom) sets how much, the pattern and the twist run on across the joint, a lip holds it in the opening, and “Pegador (impresso à parte)” adds a knob that is glued into a hole on top. “Criar acessórios” lays the parts out beside the vase as objects of their own, ready to print, upside down where that prints better. The vase already has the sockets, groove or thread. After changing a setting, lay them out again: the parts from before are replaced. If a part does not fit this vase, the editor says so, for example when an insert would not get through a narrow neck. The card “Impressão” tells what the vase takes to print: its weight in the chosen “Material” and the length of filament – for a solid vase worked out for the slicer's vase mode, one line along the wall. Below are notes on printing it: an overhang of more than 45° and where it is, a wall that is too thin, what a lid, a lamp or legs need, and the slicer settings for ribs and a double wall. A teapot lid is checked as it prints, upside down on its top: there a shoulder that narrows towards the rim overhangs. “Nível de detalhe” sets how finely the vase is divided into triangles: finer looks smoother, but makes the editor slower with large vases.
Selecting shapes, finding them in the object list, aligning, mirroring, rotating, laying flat on a face and multiplying in patterns.

A click on a shape selects it. With Shift you add more or take them away again. While Shift is held and two or more shapes are selected, a small number below the mouse pointer counts them. A click on empty space clears the selection, and so does Esc. Drag a frame on the empty workplane to select everything it touches; with Shift held, the frame adds what was not selected and takes away what was. If you would rather pick one part out of a cluster, switch on “A direção da moldura define a seleção” in the settings (area “Aparência”): a frame dragged to the right then takes only what lies completely inside it, one dragged to the left still everything it touches, and its line is dashed. Hold Alt while you drag to turn the frame around for that one drag, for example to take whole bodies from the side where the direction would not allow it. And Ctrl+A selects all visible bodies. While you drag a body or a handle of the frame, Esc cancels as long as the mouse button is still held: everything goes back as it was, and nothing is added to the history. A shape behind another one, such as a hole inside a body, you reach without turning the view: right-click the spot and choose “Selecionar outro…”. The menu then lists every shape under the pointer, from front to back. The one your pointer is on is outlined in the view, even through the shapes in front of it; a click selects it, and with Shift it is added to the selection. The entry is there whenever more than one shape lies under the pointer; on a tablet, a long press opens the same menu. What is in your way you hide (“Ocultar selecionados”, Ctrl+H). Hidden shapes stay in the design, they are just not visible and stay out of the export; the export window says beforehand how many there are. Ctrl+Shift+H brings them all back. What should stay put you lock with the padlock at the top of the settings or with Ctrl+L. A locked shape cannot be moved, resized, turned, recoloured or deleted: its handles turn grey, a padlock shows beside the arrow on top, and the tools that would change it are greyed out. Hovering a handle still shows its sizes, and a key that would change it says "Object locked". While one locked shape is in the selection, nothing changes for the others either. Hiding, renaming, copying and duplicating still work. To keep a part as it is and still build with it, lock only its shape: the shield beside the padlock, “Lock shape” in the right-click menu, or Ctrl+Shift+L. It can still be moved, turned, lifted, lined up, copied and grouped with others, but its size, its settings and its name stay as they are: the handles that change its size are gone, the fields for them are greyed out, and resizing, mirroring, ungrouping, the edge tools and deleting are refused. A copy keeps the lock, and so does the part inside a group, which can then be moved and taken apart again but not resized. The object list has the shield as well, beside the padlock: a part whose shape is locked always shows it, the others show it on the selected row and under the mouse, and a click on it locks or unlocks the shape. To work on a few parts deep inside a design, select them and choose “Hide others” in the right-click menu or under “Opções de visibilidade”: everything else is hidden in one step, so Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+Shift+H brings it back. “Invert selection” in the right-click menu selects every visible shape that was not selected and lets go of the ones that were. Both are in the command search (Ctrl+K) as well, where you can also give them a key of your own. A number on the button of the group “Visibilidade” says how many shapes are hidden, and a click on it shows them all again. A design that is opened with hidden shapes says so once, with a button to show them. A part you hide while a group is open stays hidden when you close it with “Concluído”: the group keeps its size and the parts left stay as they are, the hidden part still counts when the group is aligned, and showing all hidden shapes leaves it alone. Open the group again to show it.

With many parts it is easy to lose track in the view. The object list (“Mostrar lista de objetos” or Ctrl+Shift+O) shows all shapes as a list. It stays open or closed as you left it, for every design, until you close it; the choice is kept in the browser. The object list: the group "Group" with two parts and a sphere beside it. A folder icon opens the group. A click on an entry selects the shape, including parts inside a group. With Shift held you add more entries or take them away again, just as in the view. The arrows fold groups open and shut. The label shows whether a part is “Sólido” or “Buraco”. Under the name stands what kind of shape it is. A body that is no longer a plain shape (rounded, hollowed or imported) says “Corpo exato” when the STEP export writes it exactly, and “Malha” when it is only triangles and goes as STL. A taper, lean or twist set after rounding or hollowing a body bends only its mesh, so it then says “Malha”. Padlock and eye lock and hide single parts. “Renomear” gives a part a name of its own; the pencil beside the name at the top of the settings does the same for the selected shape. Sensible names help enormously in larger designs. The A–Z button in the title bar (“Ordenar formas com nome de A a Z”) sorts the shapes you have named alphabetically, with numbers counted as numbers (Part 2 before Part 10). Shapes that still carry their default name stay below in the order you added them, the newest last, and parts inside groups are sorted the same way. Only the list changes, never the design. A second click shows everything in the order added again, and the browser remembers the choice. The handle at the left of a row (six dots) moves a shape in the list: drag it up or down, or focus it and press ↑ or ↓. That changes the design's own order, the one the list returns to when the A–Z sort is off, and Undo takes it back. With the A–Z sort or a search on, the handles are hidden. To put a shape into a group, fold the group open with its arrow and drag the shape by its handle onto the group's parts; the group gets an orange frame. The shape stays where it is and keeps its name, and so does the group: a group is merged again with it, a bundle just takes it in. The parts of a folded-open group have a handle of their own: drag one out of the group and it lies loose again, at the place in the list where you drop it, or drop it on another folded-open group to move it there. A group left with one part is gone and leaves that part. Undo takes each of these back in one step. While you are editing a group, this is off. The search field finds shapes by name and by kind, so also "cylinder" or "hole". It also looks inside groups, however deeply nested: a group holding a match stays in the list and folds open to show the matching parts and the groups that lead to them. A group found by its own name shows all its parts when you open it. The arrow on the far left of the title bar folds the list down to its title bar and back. The list sits docked just right of the view cube. Drag it by its title bar to put it anywhere on the workplane; it passes underneath the view cube and the view bar. Drop it back beside the view cube, or double-click the title bar, and it docks again. Where it was and whether it was folded are remembered in this browser.

The card “Posição” in the properties panel shows where the selected body stands, and you can type it: “X” and “Y” are the middle of its box on the plate, with the same signs as the distances shown on the workplane, and “Z (altura)” is the height of its underside. With “Referência” at the top of the card you switch to “Borda”: X and Y then show the body's left and front edges, so you put an edge exactly on a measure. The setting stays until you switch back to “Centro”. X counts to the right, Y towards the back and Z up, by the right-hand rule as in Tinkercad and CAD programs; the axis arrows on the plate show the directions. The values go in the unit you set, and the sliders reach as far as dragging does.

You can drag a shape past the edge of the plate and leave it there, about one plate width beyond each side, to keep it for later. The arrow keys move it as far as you like. A parked part still belongs to the design and goes into the export with everything else. To leave it out, hide it or export only the selection. If you have picked a printer, layerling warns at export when something sits outside its plate.

When you drag a shape across the workplane, it snaps to other shapes: its left, right, front or back edge or its centre lands exactly on an edge or centre of another shape. A pink guide line shows what it is holding on to. That way two parts sit flush side by side or centred one behind the other without typing numbers. It works with the grid switched off, too. The centre of the workplane counts too: the pink lines show when the shape sits in the middle of the plate along X, along Y or both. Hold Shift while dragging to keep the move on one axis: the shape follows whichever direction, X or Y, you have dragged further in, and leaves the other alone. Best press Shift once you are already dragging; on a shape that is not selected yet, a click with Shift only adds it to the selection. Or pull the red or the green arrow on top of the selection: it moves along X or along Y only, and the shape follows the mouse along that line even in a low view, where a free drag runs off far. The arrows snap as a drag does, Alt lets go, and afterwards you can click the distance moved and type the exact value. With Alt already held when the drag begins, you drag a copy, as in Tinkercad: the shape stays where it is and the copy lands where you let go. Pressing Alt only on the way pauses snapping; the shape then follows the grid only. A copy, too, snaps only once you let go of Alt on the way. To switch snapping off for good, use the grid menu in the bottom right (“Encaixar em formas”) or the settings. For now only moving on the normal workplane snaps, not lifting and not resizing.

Two or more selected shapes are lined up with “Alinhar” (L, or right-click the selection and choose it): points appear around the selection for left, centre and right, front, centre and back, and top, centre and bottom. A click on a point moves all shapes there. If you first click one of the selected shapes, it stays in place and the others line up with it. A locked shape in the selection is that fixed shape by itself. Left, right, front, back, top and bottom go by the box round a shape; the centre of a triangle, a pentagon or a star is its own middle, so a hole centred on one sits in the middle of the shape and not of its box. A shape turned at an angle, say by 45°, has its box round it to line up with, not its own edges. To line up with the edges, set a workplane on a face of that shape first (“Posicionar plano de trabalho”, then click the face): the points then stand on the axes of that plane, and the shapes are measured and moved along them, as in Tinkercad. Reset the workplane to line up along the plate again. Align shows the possible targets as dots around the selection. The key is L. Esc cancels.

Hold Alt while aligning and the dots turn into squares: a click no longer moves the shapes but changes their size. A dot at a side stretches each shape to that side, its other side staying where it is, as if you had dragged its handle there. The dot in the middle leaves each shape in its place and gives it the width, length or height in that direction. That way you swap a box for a cylinder of the same size, say, or replace a broken piece of a mesh with a clean shape. Move over a dot with Alt held and you see beforehand how large the shapes become. The reference is the shape you clicked first; only the others change. Without one, the side dots stretch all shapes to the farthest side, and the middle dot gives them all the size of the largest. A cylinder stays round, so it grows in the other direction too. A shape turned at an angle stays as it is; shapes turned by 90° work.

Beside the middle point of each line stands a wider dot with a bar on each side. It spreads three or more shapes in that direction so that the space between neighbouring edges is the same everywhere, whatever size each shape is. The first and the last shape stay where they are, the ones between move. A row of holes of different sizes gets the same wall between them, for example. Move over the dot and you see beforehand where the shapes go; the status bar then tells you the gap. If a board (a base the others stand on, such as a flat box, not an SBC board) is among the selected shapes, longer in that direction than all the others, the shapes are spread on it: the gap at its edges is as large as the one between them, and a single shape comes to its middle. Shapes in several rows, such as the animals of a peg puzzle, are spread row by row; shapes whose boxes overlap across the direction form one row. Where the shapes stand in no clean columns, as the animals do from front to back, the shapes standing side by side move as a whole row instead. The whole puzzle then takes one click from left to right and one from front to back. Without a board, hold Shift and click an empty spot of the plate first: the plate is then the fixed shape, equal gaps spread the shapes over the whole plate with the same gap to its edges, and the other dots line them up on its edges or its middle. Another click with Shift on the empty plate lets it go. A click on empty space without Shift ends Align, as L and Esc do. Hold Alt and click the dot to type the gap yourself, say 5 mm: the shapes line up that far apart, starting at the first shape or at the one you clicked first; on a board the row comes to its middle. A locked shape stays where it is, so one between the outer shapes stops the equal gaps.

“Espelhar” (M, or right-click the selection and choose it) flips the selection across a plane: “esquerda-direita”, “frente-trás” or “cima-baixo”. Click the matching axis arrow. That is handy for symmetric parts: build one half, copy it and mirror the copy.

You rotate with the curved arrows on the shape, with the numbers in the settings or with R in 45° steps. When you drag on the rotation circle, the turn snaps to every tick, that is every 22.5°; hold Shift for finer steps, and extra ticks appear every 11.25°. Drag outside the circle to turn freely in 1° steps, or in 45° steps with Shift. Normally the selection turns about its centre. Sometimes it should not, for example when a tilted tube is to be turned further at its end. For that there is “Definir ponto de rotação”: afterwards click on a face. A flat face supplies its centre, for example the axis of a tube end. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body, and the pivot goes to the middle of the whole face once the parts are joined, except on a group or bundle with text in it, or a bundle with a hole among its parts. The selection now turns about that point. A second click on the tool removes it again. The angles stay with the body. In its settings, “Rotação” shows them as “Em torno de X”, “Em torno de Y” and “Em torno de Z (altura)”, named like the position: Y runs across the plate, Z is up. Type an angle there and the body turns to it - about its centre, or about its own pivot if it has one. While a turned body is selected, its angles also show below it on the workplane; “Mostrar os ângulos de sólidos girados” in the settings switches that off. A body turned about two axes: its angles stand under it, and the Rotation card in its settings takes them as numbers. With one body selected, the pivot belongs to that body: select other parts and come back, and it is still there. It moves, turns and scales with the body, is saved in the project and comes back with Undo. Under “Posição” the pivot has its own X, Y and Z, which you can type or nudge, and “Remover” takes it away. You can also drag the pivot's red marker with the mouse: it slides over the surface of the bodies and snaps to corners, edge midpoints and edges, so a hinge pin lands exactly on a corner. With several bodies selected the pivot is only for that selection, and a new selection removes it. Grouping or bundling them keeps it: the group takes the pivot as its own, with X, Y and Z under “Posição”. Hold Shift while dragging the red marker and it snaps to the centre of the face under the pointer instead - the axis of a round face, the middle of a flat one or the tip of a cone - looking through transparent bodies.

Should a part lie on its best side for printing? Select it, click “Deitar sobre a face” and then the face that should go down. While you move the pointer over the part, the face under it lights up, so you see which one you are about to pick; turn the view to check the other sides. The part turns so that this face rests on the workplane. Two parts should meet face to face, or line up flush? Select the part that should move, click “Alinhar faces”, then click its face and after that the face of the other part. In the tool window, “Face com face” puts the faces against each other (back to back, touching), “Rente” lays them in one plane side by side; “Espaço” leaves room between them, for example for clearance. “Alinhar” moves the part: it turns the shortest way until the faces are parallel - not at all if they already are - and then slides only towards the other face, so it keeps its place sideways. The other part stays where it is, and one Undo takes it all back. The Align faces tool window: the part that moves is picked, a face of the other part comes next, then face to face or flush, and an optional gap. Holes on one axis: “Mesmo eixo” lines up round faces instead: a hole over a hole, a pin in a hole, a screw in its clearance hole. Choose it before you click the faces. Then click the round inside of a hole (or the outside of a pin) on the part that moves, and a round face of the other part; the whole round face lights up while you point at it. “Alinhar” turns the part the shortest way until the two axes are parallel and slides it straight across onto the other axis. Along the axis it stays where it was, so a pin keeps its height; push it in afterwards. This works on imported meshes too, as long as the hole is made of facets around one axis. A point onto a point: “Point to point” moves the part straight, without turning it, so that one of its points lands on a point of another part. Click a corner, a spot on an edge, the centre of a round edge or a reference point on the part that moves, then the point where it should land; a dot shows which point the pointer would take. Under “Move along” switch off the axes it should not move along: with only X and Y on, the point ends up straight above or below the other; with only Z on, at the same height. One Undo takes it back. Turning by a second and third pair: after “Alinhar” the panel stays open for a second pair of points. The first point stays where it landed, marked in blue, and “Turn” turns the part about it until the line through its second point runs through the point you picked on the other part - so two edges come to lie on one line, even when the parts are not the same length. A third pair turns the part about the line through the two blue points until its third point faces the third point you picked, so the faces line up too - like aligning by three points in other CAD programs. “Done” ends it at any step; each step is one Undo. An exact angle between two faces: “Alinhar faces” leaves the faces parallel; there is no tool of its own for an angle between them, but this gets you there. First bring the faces together with “Alinhar faces”, so they are parallel. Then set the pivot on the edge where they meet (“Definir ponto de rotação”, click the edge or a corner) and type the angle, 15 or 30 say, in the “Rotação” card of the part. It turns about that pivot. The card's axes are the axes of the plate, so this works when the edge runs along X, Y or Z. Just as simple are “Baixar até o plano de trabalho” (D), which drops the selection onto the workplane, and “Centralizar no plano de trabalho”. With the workplane on a face, it centres on the point you picked with W and moves the selection only along that face, so what stands on it stays on it. Alt+D drops several parts as one piece: they all go down by the same distance and so keep their heights to each other, while D drops every part on its own. C picks the selection up, like Cruise in Tinkercad: it follows the mouse pointer and lies down on the face of another body you are over, sloped ones too. A click sets it down there, Esc leaves it where it was. Its underside then rests on the face, lined up with the face's edges as a new shape would be; it keeps its own turn about its up axis. Several parts travel together and keep their spacing. Over the empty plate, C stands a tilted part upright on the workplane again. Holding Shift while you carry sinks the part into the face instead: it stays upright, its top flush with the face and the body below it, which is how a countersink or a counterbore goes into a body; a new shape from the library is placed the same way with Shift held. Shift+D drops the selection with its top on the workplane instead of its base. Without a keyboard, the menu of a long press has “Colocar sobre uma face” for the same.

For hole grids, bolt circles and rings of teeth there is the “Padrão”. Select the shapes to be multiplied and click it in the ribbon. The pattern in "Circle" mode: the copies first appear as a preview. “Fileira”: The selection is repeated at equal distances. The row steps along all three axes at once, with “Espaçamento X”, “Espaçamento Y” and “Espaçamento Z (altura)”: one of them gives a straight row, two or three a diagonal row or a staircase. A negative spacing lays the row the other way. “Distribuir sobre um sólido”: For holes along a plate, a key holder or a coat rack. Put the first piece on or into the body, choose “Ao longo de X” or “Ao longo de Y” and set the “Espaço até a borda”: the original moves that far in from the nearer end (from the edge to the piece's side), and the last copy keeps the same gap to the far end. The spacing then follows the “Quantidade (com o original)”: five holes or nine, they always fill the plate evenly. “Grid”: For the holes of a perforated plate or a field of equal pieces. “Columns along X (with original)” and “Espaçamento X” lay the columns side by side, “Rows along Y (with original)” and “Espaçamento Y” the rows from front to back. One column or one row gives a single line. A grid has at most 100 pieces; past that the rows are cut back, and the window says so. “Círculo”: The selection is spread around a centre. How many copies there are you set under “Quantidade (com o original)”, and the “Ângulo total” is 360° for a full circle. Choose whether the copies turn along. “Subida por cópia” lifts every copy a little more than the one before (a screw or an ascending spiral), and “Mudança de raio por cópia” moves it further from the centre or closer to it (a flat spiral); together they give a conical spiral. A spiral winds once around at most: an angle above 360° counts as a full circle, and there are at most 100 copies. Tip: first set the pivot on a face with “Definir ponto de rotação”, then the centre of the circle lies exactly there. Afterwards the pieces keep the circle's centre as their pivot, also once grouped. That is where another part belongs, for example a ball in the middle of three legs: the middle of the pieces' box is not the centre, since three legs fill a box wider one way than the other. Right-click the pieces and choose “Marcar o pivô”, and the centre of the part you drag snaps onto it. The pattern in "Circle" mode with a rise and a radius change per copy: the copies climb and widen like a spiral. The copies first appear as a preview. Only “Criar” creates them. If the copies are holes, group them afterwards with the body they should cut into. With “Agrupar cópias” ticked, “Criar” groups the original and all copies into one object in the same step, as “Grupo de união” would: a ring of 36 pieces is then one part you can move, colour or cut with. Above 5 pieces the box ticks itself; once you tick or untick it yourself, it stays as you set it. “Desagrupar” brings the pieces back. If grouping does not work out, the pattern still comes in as separate pieces and the message says why.

For vents, speaker grilles, baskets and enclosures the “Padrão de furos” spreads holes evenly over a flat face or round the wall of a cylinder. You no longer have to make one hole, repeat it and set it onto the wall. Select exactly one body and click “Padrão de furos” in the “Modificar” group of the ribbon, next to the pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. The whole flat face around your click counts, not just the triangle under the pointer. The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore works too, see below; any other curved face does not: you get a hint and click a flat one instead. On a group or a bundle a face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body; on a bundle only when no hole is among them. The parts are joined shortly after the tool opens; until then only one part's face lights up under the pointer, and a click waits for the join. On a group or bundle with text in it, only one part's face lights up, and the click joins the parts. In the window, set how the holes look and lie: “Forma do furo”: “Redondo”, “Quadrado”, “Retângulo”, “Hexágono” or “Oblongo”. Size: the “Diâmetro (Ø)” of a round hole, the “Comprimento do lado” of a square one, “Largura” and “Altura” for a rectangle and a slot. For the hexagon the size is the “Diâmetro entre cantos (Ø)”. “Ângulo dos furos”: rectangles and slots only: turns every hole in the face by that many degrees, counter-clockwise as you look at the face, from -90 to 90. The rows stay straight; if turned holes would come too close, even diagonally, layerling widens the spacing and the row spacing so a wall stays between them. “Inclinação através da parede”: flat faces only, not with a counterbore, countersink or own shape: slopes every hole through the wall, from -60 to 60 degrees. On a standing wall a positive slope puts the inner end higher, so rain runs back out. The size stays the hole's own, so it shows a little longer on the face; both ends of each hole keep the margin. A slope only hides the inside when the wall thickness times sin(angle) is at least the hole's height, so use low slots or a thicker wall for that. “Own shape”: repeats a shape from the scene in place of a hole: a rivet, a stud or the tread of a diamond plate. Choose it under “Shape from the scene”. Its width and depth are the room it takes; it stands upright on the face as it was made, without its own turn. A body is set onto the face and joins it, a hole is cut in as deep as it is high. The shape itself stays where it is. “Hole type”: round holes only. “Plain” is a straight hole, “Rebaixo” adds a pocket for a cap screw's head, “Escareado” a 90° cone for a countersunk screw. The size is then the “Diâmetro do corpo”; “Diâmetro da cabeça” and, for the counterbore, “Profundidade da cabeça” set the head. “Tamanho do parafuso” fills them all in for a metric screw. “Espaçamento centro a centro”: the distance from one hole's middle to the next. If it is smaller than the holes allow, layerling raises it to the smallest possible value so a wall stays between the holes. For rectangles and slots it counts along the row, from left to right. “Espaçamento entre fileiras (centro a centro)”: rectangles and slots only: the distance from one row to the next. So narrow, tall holes stand close side by side while the rows keep apart. A hole 2 mm wide and 14 mm high needs 4 mm along the row and 16 mm from row to row with a 2 mm wall. “Parede entre os furos”: the same distance said another way: the wall left between two neighbouring holes, which is the wall thickness in the print. Set it and the spacing centre to centre follows (for rectangles and slots the row spacing too), and the other way round. For hexagons, rectangles and slots layerling measures the least distance between their edges. “Disposição”: “Grade” puts the holes in rows and columns. “Intercalada” shifts every second row by half a spacing and moves the rows closer, so every hole has neighbours at the same distance - with hexagons that makes a honeycomb. “Along the edge”: a ring of holes along the outer edge of the face instead, “Margem até a borda da face” in from it - screw holes round a lid or a plate. “Spread by” “Spacing” keeps about the spacing, “Number” sets the “Number of holes”; either way the spacing is evened out so the ring closes without a gap. “A hole on every corner” (on at first) puts a hole on each corner and shares every side out evenly between them. On a round face, or with the box unticked, the holes go evenly round from the top, and “Start along the edge” moves the whole ring along the edge. “Margem até a borda da face”: the clear distance between the holes and the edge of the face. Only holes that lie wholly inside the face minus this margin are made; anything that would reach beyond it is left out. The margin also holds around openings in the face. “Profundidade”: “Atravessando o sólido inteiro” (the default) cuts through the whole wall. With “Profundidade personalizada” you give the depth in millimetres, for recesses, say. The holes show at once as a preview on the face and follow every value. The window says how many holes fit. “Outra face” chooses another face, Esc closes the tool, and like the other tool windows it moves by its title bar. Only “Criar” makes the holes. The holes are ordinary holes grouped with the body, just as after “Grupo de união”: nothing is baked in. “Desagrupar” dissolves the group again and frees every hole, which you can then move, change or delete one by one. The whole thing is one step for “Desfazer”. The tool does not make more than 400 holes at once; make the holes bigger or the spacing wider then. The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore takes holes too: a pen holder, a lamp shade, a tube with vents. Click the wall instead of a flat face; the whole wall lights up under the pointer. Every hole then points straight at the axis, and the rows go round the wall. On a wall that goes all the way round, each row holds a whole number of holes, evened out so the ring closes without a gap and never closer than the spacing; the window says how many go round and how far apart. The margin holds to the rims at the top and the bottom and to openings in the wall, on a part of a wall (a rounded edge, say) to its sides as well. “Atravessando a parede” cuts through the one wall you clicked and leaves the far side of a tube whole; on a solid cylinder the holes go in to its middle. Clicked inside a bore, the holes go outward through its wall. “Along the edge” is for flat faces and is not offered on a wall. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_perforate_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

h: Pushing a face out or in
t: For a thicker wall, a raised pad on a face or a pocket cut into it, the “Face” tool works on one flat face. It works on an imported STL too, where there is no sketch to change. Select exactly one body and click “Face” in the “Modificar” group of the ribbon, next to the hole pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K. Click a flat face of the body. As with the hole pattern, the whole flat face around your click counts; a curved face does not work here, a round wall neither. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as with the hole pattern. In the window: “Direção”: choose “Para fora: adicionar material” for material standing on the face or “Para dentro: cortar uma cavidade” for a pocket cut into it. A pocket goes no deeper than the body behind the face; on a hollow body it can still reach the cavity. “Recuo a partir da borda da face”: how far the new outline stays inside the face's edge. Going out, 0 takes the whole face, which makes a wall thicker. Openings in the face grow by the same amount. “Raio dos cantos”: rounds every corner of the outline, the inner ones too, so a sharp tip ends in an arc. A notch narrower than twice the radius closes, and a part of the face narrower than twice the inset and the radius together is left out. “Profundidade”: how far the new part stands out of the face, or how deep the pocket goes. “Como um sólido próprio (não agrupado)”: with the switch on, the new part (or the hole of a pocket) is a body of its own beside the body instead of a group with it, so you can resize it, move it or use it to cut at once. The result shows at once as a preview and follows every value. “Outra face” chooses another face, Esc closes the tool. Only “Criar” makes it. What the tool adds is an ordinary sketch body, grouped with the body unless “Como um sólido próprio (não agrupado)” is on (then “Editar grupo” has nothing to open, and the part is free): nothing is baked in. “Editar grupo” opens the group, and “Editar esboço” on the new part shows the outline it follows. On the top or the bottom of a plain sketch body - one area, not grouped, mirrored, tapered, twisted or leaning, and without a stroke, key ring, fillet or chamfer - that is the body's own outline, set in when it is built, so its lines and arcs stay exact wherever the CAD kernel can set them in, for the edge tools and the STEP export. Resized later, the part keeps its inset. On any other face, and on every face of an imported mesh, the outline follows the face's triangles, and a curve is made of short straight pieces. The whole thing is one step for “Desfazer”. To change the inset or the radius later, undo and run the tool again. To round the top edge afterwards, use “Arredondamento” with “Arestas de cima” on the group as the last step: like every edge treatment on a group, it joins the group into one body. An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_push_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

With several parts selected, the properties panel on the right shows how many there are and offers what applies to all of them together: “Sólido” or “Buraco”, one colour for all (a click on “Sólido” opens the colours) and the lock. With a mixed selection, one click makes them all solids or all holes. If any of the parts is locked, only the lock can be used. Sizes are changed with the handles, with “Redimensionar por porcentagem” or by typing a number into a size label. With several parts the number is the size of the whole selection: every part grows with it, the spaces between them too, as when you drag a handle. Solid and hole also work with a right-click or the S and H keys.

To make one or several parts larger or smaller by the same share, say all the parts of a print file by 20 %, use “Redimensionar por porcentagem”. Select the parts, right-click them and choose “Redimensionar por porcentagem”, or search for it with Ctrl+K. Under “Novo tamanho” you type the new size as a percentage of the current one: 120 % is a fifth larger, 50 % half the size. Width, depth and height change alike, so the proportions stay. The bottom stays where it is, so nothing sinks into the plate. With several parts you choose how they grow: “Juntas”: The parts grow around their common centre, and the gaps grow with them. The whole becomes larger as if it were one part. “Cada uma no lugar”: Every part grows where it stands, and the gaps between them stay the same. The percentage field has the focus when the window opens, so from the keyboard it is Ctrl+K, the percentage, Enter; Esc closes the window. Only “Redimensionar” (or Enter in the field) changes the design, and one step back undoes it. With a locked part in the selection it does not open.

“Desfazer” (Ctrl+Z) and “Refazer” (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) step through your history. How many steps travel with the saved design you set in the settings under “Histórico”. Point at either button and its tooltip names the step it would take back or bring again, with the measure where the step has one, such as "Rounded the edges of Box (5 mm)" or "Moved 3 objects (12 mm)"; the message after the step says the same. To go back several steps at once, use the history view below. A message that reports a step just taken, such as "3 shapes deleted", has an Undo button that takes exactly that step back.

“Histórico”, next to undo and redo, opens a view of your history without changing anything. The work area shows the design as it was, and a slider at the bottom runs through every undo step: all the way to the right is the current state, each step to the left is one undo earlier, and states you have undone sit to the right of the current one. The arrow keys step through the states, Esc returns to the current state. The mouse wheel over the slider does the same, one state per notch, up to an earlier one; Page Up and Page Down jump ten states, Home goes to the oldest state and End back to the current one. You can turn and zoom the view meanwhile and click objects to bring them back (see below), but nothing can be moved; the design itself stays exactly as it is. If the bar covers something, drag it away by its title bar; a double-click on it brings it back. The list button in the title bar shows every step by name in a list, the newest at the top: a click on a step goes to that state, the state the design is at is marked “agora”, and steps you have undone are grey. The list stays open the next time if you leave it open. The two play buttons under the slider run the history like a film: the one pointing right plays forwards from the state shown, the one pointing left plays backwards, each state for a moment, until the end; pressing the same button again pauses, and moving the slider, the wheel, the keys or the list takes over. Started at the end of its way, it begins again from the other end. “Speed” sets how long each state stays (slow, normal or fast) and is remembered for next time. Record the screen while it plays to show how a part came about. Two things you can take along from an earlier state. “Novo projeto a partir deste estado” puts that state into a new design in the overview, named after this one with the time of that state in brackets - a design saved before layerling recorded times says "copy" instead - and with the history up to that point, so undo keeps working there. “Exportar este estado” opens the usual export with that state as the design, so you can save it as STL, 3MF, STEP, a picture or a LYL file with the history up to that state. You can also bring single objects back into the design. Click an object in the state shown - Shift+click adds more or takes one off again, a click on empty space picks nothing - and choose “Trazer para o projeto”. The view closes and a copy of each object lands in the current design exactly as it was in that state and at the spot it had there, selected, next to whatever the design holds now; nothing else changes. It is one step, so undo takes it back. Use it for a version of a part you changed since, or for one you deleted. A group comes back whole; notes and reference points on an object stay behind. Its name carries the time of that state, such as “Box (12:32)”, so it is easy to tell from the version the design has now. To bring back a part from inside a group, select the group and choose “Abrir grupo” or press E, as in the design: its parts are laid out where editing the group would put them, ready to pick, and the bar says which group you are in. “Sair” closes it again. This is only to look - the group, the design and the history stay as they are. “Excluir histórico” sits alone at the bottom left of the bar. After a question it removes every earlier step for good: the design keeps the state it has now (not the one shown), Undo has nothing to go back to and a file saved afterwards carries no history. Use it to share a design without its past, or to start the undo steps over. It cannot be undone; to share a file without touching your own design, choose “Nenhum” when exporting instead.

Como formas simples viram furos, rasgos e cavidades, e como alterar um grupo de união depois. Esta é a ideia mais importante do layerling, e ela se aprende rápido: toda forma é um sólido ou um buraco. Um sólido fica. Um buraco é uma ferramenta que tira material.

Selecione uma forma e clique em “Sólido” ou “Buraco” no painel de propriedades. Pelo teclado é mais rápido: H transforma a seleção em buraco, S a transforma de novo em sólido. As duas opções também estão no menu que aparece com um clique direito no sólido. Um buraco aparece transparente, para você ver onde ele está. T deixa um sólido transparente, por exemplo para olhar dentro de uma carcaça; pressione T de novo para deixá-lo opaco. Com vários sólidos selecionados, T vale para todos: se pelo menos um já estiver transparente, todos ficam opacos; se nenhum estiver, todos ficam transparentes. Enquanto nada estiver agrupado, um buraco não faz nada. Ele só fica ali e mostra onde algo vai sumir depois. O cilindro é um buraco. Ele sai pelo topo do cubo, para atravessá-lo de ponta a ponta.

Selecione os sólidos e os buracos e clique em “Grupo de união” (Ctrl+G). Agora os buracos tiram o material dos sólidos em que tocam. O que sobra é uma única forma nova. O resultado: um cubo com um furo. É assim que se fazem: Furos: um cilindro como buraco atravessando um sólido. Rasgos: uma caixa alongada como buraco na borda. Cavidades: um buraco que não atravessa até o outro lado. Roscas numa peça: um furo roscado como buraco, veja Roscas e mecânica. Se houver vários sólidos no grupo de união, eles se juntam. Dois sólidos que se tocam viram uma única peça. Com malhas grandes, como um STL importado com centenas de milhares de triângulos, o corte leva alguns segundos. layerling então trabalha em segundo plano e mostra "“Calculando… você pode continuar trabalhando”"; enquanto isso, você pode girar a vista e usar a interface. Se você alterar o modelo nesse meio-tempo, o resultado é descartado e layerling avisa. O mesmo vale para “Dividir”. Um grupo de união pode ser tratado como uma forma: mover, girar, mudar a cor, agrupar de novo. “Desagrupar” (Ctrl+Shift+G) desfaz o grupo de união, e as peças voltam a ficar separadas.

h: Transformando um grupo de união em buraco
t: Um grupo de união inteiro também pode ser um sólido ou um buraco. Vale uma regra simples: Se o grupo de união tem só sólidos (ou só buracos), você o troca por inteiro e as peças acompanham. Se tem os dois, por exemplo um cubo com um furo, cada peça mantém o seu próprio estado. O grupo de união inteiro vira então uma ferramenta, mas o furo continua sendo um furo.

h: Redimensionando um grupo de união: mantendo furos e peças pequenas
t: Quando um grupo de união fica mais comprido, mais largo ou mais alto, as peças se esticam junto, como se estivessem desenhadas em borracha: os furos redondos de uma placa viram ovais e se deslocam para dentro. Para mantê-los como estão, escolha “Keep holes and small parts” em “When resized” nas configurações do grupo; “Stretch everything” é o que todo grupo faz até você mudar. A partir daí, cada vez que o grupo é redimensionado - pelas alças, pelos campos de tamanho ou por “Redimensionar por porcentagem” - ele é montado de novo a partir das peças por uma única regra, em cada direção separadamente: Uma peça que atravessa quase o grupo inteiro, nove décimos dele ou mais, cresce ou encolhe junto e mantém a distância aos dois lados: a própria placa, uma parede ou o interior de uma caixa, cujas paredes continuam com a mesma espessura. Todas as outras peças mantêm o próprio tamanho e a distância ao lado mais próximo. Uma peça no meio continua no meio. Assim, uma placa com um furo a 5 mm de cada canto e uma fenda no meio, aumentada em 40 mm de comprimento, mantém os furos redondos e a 5 mm dos cantos, e a fenda no meio. Não há nenhum solver por trás e nada para configurar peça por peça: a mesma regra vale para todas as peças, então dá para saber antes o que vai acontecer. Uma peça girada conta com a caixa que ocupa no grupo e continua girada; um grupo dentro do grupo conta como uma peça. Enquanto você arrasta uma alça, o grupo se estica por inteiro; ao soltar, ele é montado de novo, no mesmo passo de desfazer. Se ficar menor do que uma peça precisa com a sua distância, essa peça encolhe com o grupo como antes, e uma mensagem avisa. Um grupo espelhado, afunilado ou torcido, e um com arredondamentos, chanfros ou uma textura própria, sempre estica tudo. Escolhida para um grupo que já está esticado, a configuração reorganiza as peças na hora. Uma placa com um furo a 5 mm de cada canto e uma fenda no meio, aumentada em 40 mm de comprimento com a opção de manter furos e peças pequenas: os furos continuam redondos e a 5 mm dos cantos, a fenda continua no meio.

Às vezes as peças só devem ficar juntas, sem virar uma só, por exemplo um logotipo branco sobre uma placa preta para uma impressão multicolorida. É para isso que serve “Criar conjunto” (Ctrl+B), como no Tinkercad. Um conjunto se move, gira e muda de tamanho como uma forma, mas nada é fundido: Cada peça mantém a sua cor e continua sendo um sólido ou um buraco. No painel de propriedades, o conjunto tem os mesmos cartões de um grupo de união: “Sólido” e “Buraco” para o conjunto inteiro (que mantêm as cores das peças), “Transparente” (T) e “Multicor” (Shift+M); com “Multicor” desligado, o conjunto aparece e é exportado numa cor só. “Separar peças” desfaz o conjunto, como Ctrl+Shift+G. Os buracos não cortam nada. Quando você agrupa o conjunto com outras peças, os buracos dele cortam essas peças, mas continuam sem cortar os sólidos do próprio conjunto, como no Tinkercad. Assim, por exemplo, um pino com o seu buraco ao lado pode ser reaproveitado várias vezes como conjunto. Ao exportar em STL, 3MF ou OBJ, cada peça é um sólido separado; em 3MF e OBJ, com a sua cor. “Desagrupar” (Ctrl+Shift+G) desfaz um conjunto, e E o abre para edição, como um grupo de união. Chanfro, arredondamento e vazar não funcionam num conjunto, porque ele não é um único sólido: para isso, agrupe-o ou trabalhe nas peças uma por uma. Se um buraco do conjunto também deve cortar os sólidos do próprio conjunto, desfaça o conjunto e agrupe as peças (Ctrl+G).

“Interseção booleana” mantém só o que dois ou mais sólidos têm em comum. Coloque duas formas uma sobre a outra, sobrepostas, selecione as duas e clique em “Interseção booleana”. Assim um cilindro e uma caixa viram uma peça com um lado redondo e um lado reto. Um grupo de união entra na interseção do jeito que aparece, com os buracos já recortados. Se um buraco também estiver selecionado, o que sobra é o que todos os sólidos têm em comum com todos os buracos. Se as formas não têm nada em comum, uma mensagem informa que nada foi alterado. O primeiro clique exibe a parte em comum antes de aplicá-la: as formas selecionadas ficam transparentes, e o que elas têm em comum aparece em verde. Selecione e mova cada forma separadamente, e a parte verde acompanha; outro clique em “Interseção booleana” aplica, Esc fecha a prévia. Formas com triângulos demais para a prévia, como malhas importadas grandes, são intersectadas já no primeiro clique. “Envoltória” envolve as formas selecionadas em um único sólido convexo, como se fossem embaladas a vácuo: o menor sólido sem reentrâncias que contém todas elas. Uma meia esfera sobre um cilindro vira uma cúpula sem degrau, quatro cilindros nos cantos viram uma caixa de cantos arredondados, e duas esferas, uma cápsula. Os buracos da seleção são recortados da envoltória depois. A envoltória guarda as peças: “Editar grupo” a abre como um grupo de união, e se você mover uma peça dentro dela e clicar em “Concluído”, a envoltória é reconstruída. A envoltória é uma malha, então formas redondas mostram facetas, e as ferramentas de aresta funcionam nela como em qualquer malha. Quando só furos estão selecionados, a envoltória é ela mesma um furo: dois furos cilíndricos cortam um rasgo oblongo. A envoltória preenche tudo o que é oco em suas peças: um tubo, um cilindro esvaziado com “Vazar”, uma peça agrupada com seus furos. Ative “Manter os furos das peças” em Propriedades para mantê-los abertos: a envoltória então só preenche o espaço entre as peças, e um rebaixo na lateral de uma peça também fica. “Cortador de biscoito” transforma a seleção num cortador de biscoito: uma parede fina de 15 mm de altura ao longo do contorno e uma aba plana de 2 mm em volta da base, para o cortador se apoiar na aba e você ter onde apertar com o polegar. Se você selecionar um único SVG importado ou um único sólido de esboço, a ferramenta usa o contorno dele. No caso de um texto deitado, o contorno segue as curvas das próprias letras. Nas outras formas (uma forma montada, uma malha importada ou várias peças), o contorno vem do corte feito pelo plano de trabalho. Por isso, coloque a forma primeiro sobre o plano de trabalho. Peças que se sobrepõem geram um único contorno em volta de todas, como se estivessem agrupadas; peças separadas geram um cortador para cada uma, todos no mesmo conjunto. O contorno é espelhado da esquerda para a direita: o cortador é impresso apoiado na aba e depois virado de cabeça para baixo para cortar. Assim, o texto ou o logotipo fica na orientação certa na massa. O topo da parede afina até um fio de corte de 0,4 mm de largura. Os espaços internos do contorno, como o miolo de um e ou de um a, ganham paredes próprias, então também são recortados do biscoito. Essas paredes internas formam um sólido à parte no conjunto, chamado “Paredes internas”: para só marcar um texto ou um padrão na massa, em vez de recortá-lo, diminua a altura delas no painel de propriedades. Com uma parede de 15 mm e uma massa de 5 mm de espessura, paredes internas de 12 mm deixam uma marca de 2 mm de profundidade. Paredes internas mais baixas que a parede externa têm o topo plano em vez do fio de corte: elas só marcam, e um fio deixaria pontas finas que quebram e sulcos que prendem massa. Se quiser um fio nelas, ajuste no painel de propriedades. Duas pontes do lado da aba, onde a mão aperta, prendem cada parede interna à parede que a cerca. As pontes ficam distribuídas em volta da parede interna e têm 4 mm de largura e 3 mm de altura. Cada ponte se apoia nas paredes com toda a sua largura, no meio de um trecho que acompanha o contorno, sem atravessar outra peça. Peças lado a lado, como as letras de um nome, também são ligadas entre si, começando pelas mais próximas, de modo que as pontes formam uma rede por todas elas e até uma letra no meio de uma palavra fica presa. Um clique na ferramenta abre uma pequena janela, onde você pode escolher uma “Placa” em vez das pontes: ela preenche todo o contorno do lado em que você aperta, é mais firme e adere melhor à mesa de impressão, mas impede que você solte a massa empurrando por trás. Com “Reforços”, você cria pequenas inclinações de 45° onde as paredes se apoiam na aba, nas pontes ou na placa, para que partes finas, como o pingo de um i, não quebrem; essas inclinações formam um sólido à parte no conjunto. Na mesma janela você também define quanto reduzir a altura das paredes internas e se quer espelhar o contorno; os valores ficam guardados para o próximo cortador. Você ajusta a altura das paredes internas e da aba no painel de propriedades. O cortador substitui a seleção por um conjunto de sólidos de esboço. Use “Editar grupo” para abri-lo. A parede, as paredes internas e a aba usam os modos de preenchimento de esboço, com um traço por fora da silhueta: no painel de propriedades, você muda a espessura, a altura ou a cor de cada parte e ajusta o “Fio de corte” da parede (0 deixa o topo plano). Onde uma curva muito fechada não deixa espaço para chanfrar os dois lados, a parede é chanfrada só por fora, até o mesmo fio de corte. Onde um contorno não pode ser chanfrado de jeito nenhum (um logotipo com pontas agudas, um contorno obtido dos triângulos de um sólido), o fio de corte é feito em degraus finos de 0,1 mm, que não se distinguem da inclinação numa impressão com camadas de 0,2 mm; uma parede assim é uma malha de triângulos, e não um sólido exato. Para manter o contorno como foi desenhado, espelhe o cortador de volta com “Espelhar”, “esquerda-direita”. Uma imagem PNG ou JPG também serve: ao ser importada, ela é contornada e vira um sólido de esboço, e o cortador segue esse contorno. “Transição entre esboços” une dois sólidos de esboço ou SVGs importados em um único sólido, com o contorno do sólido de baixo na base, o do sólido de cima no topo e paredes retas entre eles. Assim você faz um funil, uma peça de transição de quadrado para redondo ou uma moldura que afunila para cima. Coloque os dois sólidos um acima do outro, na posição desejada (deslocados e girados, se quiser), selecione os dois e clique na ferramenta. A transição vai da base do sólido inferior ao topo do superior. Cada um dos dois precisa de exatamente um contorno. Se um deles tiver vãos, o outro precisa ter a mesma quantidade. A transição também liga esses vãos: dois anéis, por exemplo, formam uma peça oca. Um esboço feito como traço (traço externo, interno ou centralizado no painel de propriedades) conta como um anel desses. Um SVG importado chega preenchido; para transformá-lo em anel, escolha um dos modos de traço no painel de propriedades. Os dois sólidos precisam estar deitados; a ferramenta não aceita sólidos inclinados. A transição é um sólido CAD exato; as ferramentas de aresta e a exportação STEP a tratam como tal. Os dois esboços ficam guardados dentro dela. Use “Editar grupo” para editá-los como um grupo de união. Se você mover ou alterar um dos sólidos, ou editar seu esboço, a transição é reconstruída ao clicar em “Concluído”. “Desagrupar” separa os dois esboços de novo. Para dois retângulos, círculos ou polígonos, você também pode usar a forma Transição e definir suas extremidades com números.

Para peças que precisam encaixar, um eixo em uma bucha ou um parafuso em uma caixa, você faz uma peça e a recorta da outra. Selecione os dois sólidos e clique em “Recortar” na área “Combinar”, ou dê um clique direito e escolha “Recortar” no menu. A janela nomeia a peça que é mantida e o sólido que recebe a cavidade; layerling escolhe o menor como peça, e “Trocar os dois” inverte. “Folga” deixa a cavidade maior que a peça nessa medida, de cada lado: com 0, o encaixe é exato; 0,2 mm é uma folga comum para um encaixe impresso. “Recortar” recorta uma cópia da peça do outro sólido e deixa a própria peça onde está. O resultado é um grupo de união: “Desagrupar” separa o recorte de novo. Uma folga exige que a peça seja um sólido exato, como na ferramenta “Deslocamento”, que o recorte usa para isso.

h: Puncionando um contorno através de um sólido
t: Para cortar o contorno de um sólido em linha reta através de outro, selecione primeiro o punção e depois o sólido a puncionar e clique em “Puncionar” na área “Combinar”, ou escolha com um clique direito. Os dois não precisam se tocar: o punção pode ficar em qualquer lugar na frente do sólido, e só conta o seu contorno visto ao longo da “Direção”. Assim, um bule segurado sobre uma placa deixa nela uma abertura com a forma de um bule. layerling começa pelo eixo ao longo do qual o punção está mais longe do sólido; X vai da esquerda para a direita, Y da frente para trás, Z para cima. “Trocar os dois” inverte os papéis, e a “Folga” aumenta a abertura em todos os lados, 0,2 mm para uma peça impressa que precisa passar. “Puncionar” agrupa a abertura (um sólido de esboço exato definido como buraco) com o sólido, então “Desagrupar” a retira de novo; o punção fica onde está. Mova ou gire o punção e puncione de novo para outra abertura.

Se um furo ficou pequeno demais, você não precisa desfazer o grupo de união e montar tudo de novo. Selecione o grupo de união e clique em “Editar grupo” no painel de propriedades, no ícone de pasta na lista de objetos, ou pressione E. Na lista de objetos, você também pode expandir o grupo de união clicando na seta ao lado dele. Depois, clique numa das peças: o grupo de união se abre para edição com essa peça selecionada. Um clique duplo também abre um grupo de união ou um conjunto para edição, como no Tinkercad; se preferir que não, desligue “Clique duplo abre um grupo de união ou um conjunto” nas configurações. Uma peça só começa a se mover depois que o ponteiro foi arrastado alguns pixels, então um clique ou clique duplo tremido não a desloca. As peças agora ficam separadas, e você as altera com qualquer ferramenta: aumentar um buraco, mover um sólido, adicionar um buraco. O grupo de união em edição: a barra embaixo tem Cancelar e Concluído, e a lista de objetos mostra as peças. Uma barra aparece na parte de baixo da área de trabalho. “Concluído” reconstrói o grupo de união, com o nome, a cor e o estado de sólido ou buraco. “Cancelar” o devolve sem alterações. Se uma das peças for ela mesma um grupo de união, você pode editá-la do mesmo jeito, e assim por diante, até onde o seu projeto for. A barra mostra onde você está, por exemplo "Suporte › Ressalto do parafuso". “Concluído” e “Cancelar” sempre concluem o grupo de união mais interno e levam você um nível para fora. Enquanto você está dentro de um grupo de união, só os grupos de união entre as peças dele podem ser editados; para editar outro, conclua primeiro. Ao contrário de “Desagrupar”, que desfaz um grupo de união de vez, editar mantém o grupo: o nome e as configurações ficam, e você sempre pode voltar com “Cancelar”. Uma observação: arredondamentos e chanfros que você aplicou no grupo de união inteiro se perdem na reconstrução. A barra mostra esse aviso.

“Dividir”, na área “Modificar”, corta a seleção em duas com um plano, por exemplo uma peça grande demais para a mesa de impressão, ou uma cujo interior você quer ver. Selecione um ou mais sólidos ou buracos e clique em “Dividir”. Um plano translúcido mostra exatamente onde o corte vai passar, e uma linha branca o marca nos próprios sólidos, onde o plano os encontra; nada muda até você aplicar. “Orientação do plano”: X faz um corte vertical entre esquerda e direita, Y entre frente e trás, Z um corte horizontal entre cima e baixo. Os eixos têm os mesmos nomes do cartão Posição, com Z para cima. O plano começa paralelo ao plano de trabalho, então na mesa com Z. “Alinhar ao plano de trabalho”: “Paralelo” deita o plano paralelo ao plano de trabalho, “Transversal a X” e “Transversal a Y” o deixam em pé, perpendicular a ele, atravessando a direção X ou Y dele. Onde a origem do plano de trabalho cruza a seleção, o plano passa por essa origem; senão, pelo meio. Assim você coloca o plano de trabalho numa face inclinada com W e corta bem ali, sem mexer nos controles deslizantes. “Posição do plano”: onde o plano cruza, pelo controle deslizante ou digitando o valor. Ele começa no meio. Você também pode arrastar a ponta da seta no plano; o plano se move ao longo da seta em incrementos de 0,1 mm. “Escolher face”, o botão ao lado da posição, deita o plano sobre uma face: clique nele e depois na face. Orientação, as duas rotações e a posição são ajustadas para combinar. Enquanto você escolhe, um plano azul sob o ponteiro mostra a face que será usada. Uma face de um sólido que não está selecionado também serve, para alinhar o corte com ela, mas o plano fica dentro da seleção. Esc interrompe a escolha e deixa o plano onde estava. Os dois controles deslizantes de rotação abaixo giram o plano em torno dos outros dois eixos, até 180° para cada lado, para um corte em ângulo. Eles podem ser combinados. “Dividir modelo” ou Enter faz o corte, Esc cancela (enquanto você escolhe uma face, o primeiro Esc só interrompe a escolha). Cada objeto que o plano cruza vira dois sólidos fechados, com o nome do seu lado, por exemplo "Caixa (Z+)" e "Caixa (Z-)"; os objetos que ele não cruza ficam como estão. Um buraco vira dois buracos, e um sólido vazado mantém o seu espaço interno. As duas metades ficam onde estavam; para imprimir, deite cada uma sobre a face cortada com “Deitar sobre a face”. “Connectors” alinham as metades de novo, como fazem as ferramentas de corte do PrusaSlicer, do OrcaSlicer e do Bambu Studio. Com “None”, o padrão, a divisão é como descrito acima. “Dowels” faz um furo em cada metade e pinos soltos que entram nas duas: os pinos vêm como um terceiro sólido, em pé ao lado das metades sobre o piso, para imprimir junto - em pé, eles saem redondos nas camadas como os furos, e é isso que o teste de encaixe mede. “Plugs” coloca pinos redondos na metade cujo nome termina em menos, com os furos para eles na outra metade. Os conectores entram perpendiculares ao plano, seja qual for o giro dele, cada um com seu diâmetro e 1,2 mm de material até cada borda da face de corte, e dois deles a uma distância do dobro disso. Cada pedaço separado da face de corte recebe os seus, distribuídos por igual: “Per cut face (0 = automatic)” diz quantos, e 0 deixa isso pelo tamanho do pedaço, com pelo menos dois. Um pedaço pequeno demais para um não recebe nenhum, e um conector fica de fora onde uma metade é mais fina do que a profundidade do seu furo; o painel avisa antes de você dividir, e anéis brancos no plano mostram onde eles vão ficar. Se nenhum couber, as peças são divididas sem conectores, e a barra de status avisa. “Diameter” é o diâmetro dos pinos, 5 mm para começar. “Depth into each half” é quanto cada furo entra na sua metade. Um pino solto tem o dobro disso menos 0,6 mm de comprimento, e um pino fixo é 0,3 mm mais curto que o seu furo, para que nunca apoiem no fundo de um furo e as metades fechem por completo. Os pinos têm um pequeno chanfro nas pontas, e cada furo um na boca, para que uma primeira camada que se espalhou não o estreite. “Dowels on a breakaway base”, com “Dowels”, coloca os pinos soltos numa placa comum que adere à mesa, para impressoras cuja mesa móvel faz balançar as peças em pé.
